title: Delta's Best Product Doesn't Fly
summary: American Express paid Delta $8.2 billion in 2025, more than Delta's whole operating profit. Here's how airline miles became one of the airline's most important products.

hooks.hook: Last year, one company paid Delta $8.2 billion. It wasn't a passenger. It was a credit card company.
Delta's most important product doesn't fly.
A credit card paid Delta more than flying did.
Is Delta an airline or a credit card business with wings?
In 2020, with every plane parked, Delta borrowed $9 billion against its miles.

sources: Delta Air Lines 2025 Form 10-K (Item 1): "In 2025, remuneration from American Express totaled $8.2 billion, which we expect to grow to $10 billion over the next few years"; "Our most significant and valuable contract to sell miles relates to our co-brand credit card relationship with American Express"; "In 2025, 12% of revenue miles flown on Delta were from award travel ... approximately 35 million award tickets"; fuel cost $9,819 million: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/27904/000002790426000013/dal-20251231.htm

Delta December quarter and full year 2025 results (Jan 13, 2026): operating revenue $63.4 billion, operating income $5.8 billion (9.2% margin), pre-tax income $6.2 billion: https://news.delta.com/delta-air-lines-announces-december-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-results

Delta's $9.0 billion of financings secured by the SkyMiles program, September 2020 (Kilpatrick Townsend release): https://ktslaw.com/insights/news/news-release/2020/9/kilpatrick-townsend-advises-delta-air-lines-on-9-billion-skymiles-financings
Our calculation: $8.2B American Express remuneration / $9.819B fuel = 84%. Remuneration is revenue, not profit; it is compared with operating income only to show its size.
United's $6.8 billion financing secured by MileagePlus (July 7, 2020): https://www.kirkland.com/news/press-release/2020/07/kirkland-reps-ua-on--financing-mileageplus

United valued MileagePlus at about $22 billion, almost double its $11.7 billion market capitalization; 71% of MileagePlus cash flow in 2019 from third parties (Bloomberg, via Executive Traveller, June 2020): https://www.executivetraveller.com/news/how-united-airlines-took-a-7bn-mortgage-on-its-frequent-flyer-scheme

scenes.narration: Last year, one company paid Delta Air Lines {$8.2 billion.|eight point two billion dollars.} It wasn't a passenger. It was a credit card company.
That's more than Delta made from running the whole airline: an operating profit of {$5.8 billion.|five point eight billion dollars.}

data.title: Delta, 2025
data.source: Delta 2025 10-K and full-year results (payments are revenue, not profit)

scenes.narration: Delta took in {$63.4 billion|sixty-three point four billion dollars} last year, mostly from tickets. But its most valuable deal isn't with a passenger.
So is Delta an airline that sells a credit card, or a credit card business that happens to fly planes?
To find out, let's follow a single mile: who makes it, who buys it, and who pays for your free flight.
Part one. Miles are money.
Delta creates miles whenever it likes. It sells them to American Express. Amex hands them to you every time you spend on its Delta card.
Think of Delta as a little central bank. It prints the currency, and it decides what that currency buys.
So every swipe of a Delta card at the grocery store sends a little money to an airline.
In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} those payments reached {$8.2 billion,|eight point two billion dollars,} and Delta expects them to hit ten billion within a few years.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every Tuesday and Friday.
Part two. The seat you paid for twice.
Then you spend those miles. In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} about {12 percent|twelve percent} of all the miles flown on Delta were award trips: roughly {35 million|thirty-five million} tickets.

data.label: of miles flown were award trips

scenes.narration: And Delta decides which seats you can book with miles, and how many miles each one costs.
And Delta was paid for those miles long before anyone boarded. The card company paid when you earned them.
Here's the scale. Delta's whole fuel bill for the year was {$9.8 billion.|nine point eight billion dollars.} The card money alone covered more than four fifths of it.
Part three. When the planes stopped.
In {2020,|twenty twenty,} Delta's planes sat on the ground. The airline needed cash, fast.
So it borrowed {$9 billion.|nine billion dollars.} And the collateral wasn't its planes. It was SkyMiles, its frequent flyer program.
When flying almost stopped, lenders were still willing to bet on the miles.
And it wasn't just Delta. That same summer, United borrowed {$6.8 billion|six point eight billion dollars} against its own program, MileagePlus.
United said MileagePlus was worth about {$22 billion,|twenty-two billion dollars,} almost double what the whole airline was worth on the stock market at the time.

data.source: United's own valuation, reported by Bloomberg via Executive Traveller

scenes.narration: Why so valuable? In {2019,|twenty nineteen,} {71 percent|seventy-one percent} of MileagePlus cash came from partners like credit card companies, not from people flying.

scenes.narration: So the next time someone offers you a credit card at the gate, you're looking at one of Delta's most important products.
It doesn't fly. It keeps the airline flying. Next time: McDonald's, the landlord that sells burgers.
